Rattlesnake bites are a common veterinary emergency in North America. Rapid and accurate identification of bites from a venomous snake is crucial for guiding timely administration of antivenom and supportive care. Snake bites are not always witnesses and pet owners may have difficulty identifying the species of the snake.


Development of a rapid test to accurately identify venom in blood samples from dogs could help more accurately and readily identify venom exposure.

Feline obesity is a significant health concern affecting an estimated 15 million cats in the United States. This condition is a primary contributor to serious health problems and is closely associated with an increased risk of developing diabetes mellitus and osteoarthritis. As there are currently limited therapeutic strategies to manage weight effectively in domestic indoor cats, further research into new treatment options is essential.


OKV-119 is an investigational, first-in-class, ultra-long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist implant designed specifically for veterinary use. The implant leverages the NanoPortal\u2122 drug-delivery platform to provide continuous, smooth release of exenatide over multiple months. In laboratory studies with healthy cats, OKV-119 demonstrated sustained pharmacologic activity and was generally well tolerated, supporting evaluation in client-owned obese cats.

Feline inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and intestinal lymphoma (EATL) often cause the exact same symptoms in cats, like frequent vomiting, weight loss, or diarrhea\u2014yet they require very different treatments. Currently, getting a definitive diagnosis usually means putting a sick cat through invasive procedures like surgical intestinal biopsies.


This study is evaluating a simple, innovative blood test that looks for specific biological markers to clearly tell these two conditions apart. This new approach aims to provide families and veterinarians with a gentle, affordable, and fast diagnostic tool\u2014without the stress, cost, or recovery time of surgery.

Heart disease can be difficult for veterinarians to diagnose in dogs and cats, as the symptoms are often subtle or can be mistaken for other health issues. Currently, there are very few readily available tests to help quickly and accurately detect heart problems in pets. This study aims to address that gap by developing a new, in-house blood test that can detect heart disease. By collecting blood samples from cats and dogs with and without heart conditions, researchers will create and validate a fast and reliable diagnostic tool. The goal is to provide veterinarians with a better method for screening at-risk pets, diagnosing heart conditions earlier, and ultimately improving the health and care of pets everywhere.
